name: ffc.h
baseline: strtod (C library; the Apple silicon test machine would be using the macOS libc, which the README does not name)
workload: Lemire's simple_fastfloat_benchmark parsing ASCII decimal text into doubles: 100,000 random numbers uniform in [0.0,1.0], the canada.txt dataset (111,126 lines) and the mesh.txt dataset (73,019 lines); one 32-bit run (benchmark32) against strtof.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark output (Apple silicon, 2026-03-03), ffc vs strtod in MB/s: random [0,1] 2149.68 vs 1102.63 (1.95x, derived from page data); canada.txt 1452.90 vs 916.32 (1.59x, derived from page data); mesh.txt 1019.67 vs 605.46 (1.68x, derived from page data). 32-bit run: ffc 2288.40 vs strtof 1160.10 MB/s (1.97x, derived from page data). Versus its own upstream: ffc 2149.68 vs fastfloat 1902.52 MB/s on random numbers (1.13x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: clang for all runs except benchmark32, which the README says ran with gcc; versions and optimisation flags for the benchmark build are not stated (the repo Makefile builds its tests with clang -O3 -std=c99, but that is not the benchmark build)
hardware: Apple silicon; the benchmark prints 'loaded db: as3 (Apple silicon)' and clock readings of about 3.8-4.1 GHz, exact chip model not stated
stars_or_usage: 209 stars; README says valkey (valkey_strtod.h) and a hiredis pull request use it
tradeoffs: Single-header C99 port of fast_float's algorithm (src/ includes a bigint fallback); also parses 32/64-bit integers in bases 2-36 and offers exact fixed-notation double formatting (ffc_format_double_fixed). Needs the length of the input or an end pointer, unlike strtod. Optional macros trade safety for speed: FFC_ROUNDS_TO_NEAREST elides the runtime rounding-mode check (wrong results if code changes the rounding mode), FFC_ENABLE_FLOAT_INLINING speeds up float parsing 7-35% (README) but can slow double parsing by about 2%.
caveats: First-party numbers from one Apple silicon machine; the README shows raw benchmark output only, without compiler versions or flags, and the harness (lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark) is referenced but not opened by me. The baseline is whatever strtod the macOS libc provides, so the roughly 1.6-2x speedup says little about glibc or musl strtod, and no x86 numbers are published (the macro notes mention Linux x86/ARM measurements but give no figures). Most of the win belongs to the fast_float algorithm: ffc is a port and is only 1.06-1.13x faster than C++ fast_float in the same table. The numbers are dated 2026-03-03 while force-inlining and API changes landed later (last commit 2026-10-02), so they may not match the current header. Candidate duplicate or port of fast_float, which is already catalogued.

name: Graaf
baseline: Boost Graph Library (Boost.Graph 1.84.0, via the perf/boost benchmarks for Dijkstra, BFS, Kruskal, Prim, greedy and Welsh-Powell colouring)
workload: Graaf's perf/ executables (Google Benchmark v1.8.2, Release build) running the same algorithms in Graaf and in Boost.Graph on SNAP web-Google and web-BerkStan edge lists; per-algorithm ratios are quoted in the project's own pull requests.
claimed_speedup: NO SPEEDUP CLAIMED, AND THE NUMBERS SHOW GRAAF IS SLOWER. README says only 'doesn't sacrifice on performance' and 'lightweight alternative to the Boost Graph Library'. Pull-request numbers (web_google / web_berkstan, Graaf time relative to Boost) after the September 2026 vector-storage optimisations: Kruskal 1.14x / 1.60x slower (PR #451, was 3.48x / 3.20x); Prim 2.01x / 1.85x slower (PR #452); greedy colouring 2.13x / 7.70x slower (PR #455); Welsh-Powell 2.59x / 5.71x slower (PR #456); BFS 3.55x / 8.65x slower (PR #449); Dijkstra single path 4.38x / 12.56x slower (PR #453, still open when read); dijkstra_shortest_paths 6.94x / 17.01x slower (PR #454). Initial comparison (PR #419): Graaf 13.39 s vs Boost 1.33 s on web-Google and 14.11 s vs 0.69 s on web-BerkStan.
compiler_and_flags: Release build; compiler and flags not stated in the PRs (their tests ran on g++-12 and clang++-16 in Debug mode)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, general user-defined vertex and edge types, free-function algorithms, DOT output; storage is hash-map based (unordered_map keyed by vertex id) which the ongoing perf PRs are replacing with vectors internally while keeping unordered_map return types. Smaller algorithm set than Boost.Graph.
caveats: FLAGGED NOT FASTER: every numeric comparison against the named baseline (Boost.Graph) shows Graaf slower, from 1.14x to 17x; the project claims only a lightweight, easy-to-use alternative. The numbers are first-party PR descriptions (no hardware, no compiler version, no flags beyond 'Release'), one of them (#454) credits an AI assistant as co-author, and the benchmark code is public in perf/ (graaflib and boost directories). The gaps are moving quickly (a series of perf PRs merged 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-28, last commit 2026-09-28), so later commits may close more of the gap. Kept as a record only so the catalogue can show the evidence is negative.

name: GNU gperf
baseline: std::unordered_map (string-keyed lookup in a fixed keyword set)
workload: qlibs/mph benchmark: ns per lookup of random strings from a fixed key set (5, 6 or 100 keys; lengths 4, 8, 2-5 and 1-8) through a gperf-generated function versus std::unordered_map; separately, constexpr-phf's benchmark on Xapiand's 192 field-type names (mixed length).
claimed_speedup: GNU gperf's own manual and README give no numbers. Third-party numbers (ns/op, gperf vs std::unordered_map), clang++: 5 keys len 8: 7.70 vs 13.45 (1.75x, derived from page data); 6 keys len 2-5: 7.94 vs 15.28 (1.92x, derived); 100 keys len 8: 8.04 vs 15.32 (1.91x, derived); 100 keys len 1-8: 13.06 vs 19.34 (1.48x, derived). g++: 100 keys len 8: 7.75 vs 15.01 (1.94x, derived); 100 keys len 1-8: 11.20 vs 25.35 (2.26x, derived). Counter-example: 5 keys len 4: gperf 7.70 vs unordered_map 5.56 ns/op (clang++) and 7.69 vs 5.29 (g++), i.e. gperf 1.4x slower. Kronuz/constexpr-phf README on 192 field-type names: gperf 14 ns/op vs std::unordered_map 29 ns/op (2.07x, derived from page data) and std::set 82 ns/op.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ and g++ (versions not stated), -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mbmi2 (qlibs/mph benchmark); GCC 11 -O3 on x86_64 (constexpr-phf)
stars_or_usage: GitHub mirror has 0 stars; used by the GNU C, GNU C++, GNU Pascal and GNU Java compilers and GNU indent to recognise reserved words (gperf README and manual)
tradeoffs: Build-time generator that emits C or C++ source (switch or table form) for a fixed keyword set; the generated code is not covered by the GPL (manual, 'The Copyright of the Output'), but the generator is GPL. Works on selected character positions, so it handles small and medium sets well; gsauthof/phashtable's README reports it does not terminate in a reasonable time on 1.4 million ISINs and gave a 10% table fill on smaller sets, and rurban/Perfect-Hash's README says it cannot deal with certain anagrams. Non-minimal tables by default.
caveats: The speedup evidence comes from competing perfect-hash libraries' READMEs (qlibs/mph, Kronuz/constexpr-phf), not from the gperf project, and in both gperf is shown beaten by the authors' own library (mph 1.4-1.6 ns/op on the string rows vs gperf 7.7-13 ns/op). qlibs/mph benchmark code is public (branch 'benchmark') with compiler flags, but the CPU is not stated; constexpr-phf names GCC 11 -O3 but no CPU in the section I read. Random-string key sets only; gperf loses on 5 four-character keys. The original evidence, Schmidt's 1990 USENIX C++ paper 'GPERF: A Perfect Hash Function Generator' (Section 5 benchmarks against other keyword-lookup methods), sits on hosts blocked in this session, so its numbers are not recorded. Home page https://www.gnu.org/software/gperf/ was not reachable; the repo URL is an unofficial GitHub mirror whose latest commit is 2022-02-08 and may lag the GNU Savannah repository.

name: jemalloc
workload: ruby-alloc-bench: Ruby 4.0.6 with YJIT running yjit-bench's railsbench (Rails 8.1, sqlite) in one process with 5 threads for 1200 s x 3 rounds, allocators swapped via LD_PRELOAD in the ruby:4.0-slim-trixie image; primary metric median RSS, with req/s and p99 recorded.
claimed_speedup: jemalloc 5.3.1 vs glibc default: 1751 vs 1662 req/s (+5.4%, stated on page; 1.05x), median RSS 174.5 MB vs 183.9 MB (-5.1%), p99 17.79 ms vs 18.04 ms, 36 vs 52 major GCs, round-to-round spread 1.33%. Versus glibc with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2: 1751 vs 1639 req/s (1.07x, derived from page data). Supporting memory evidence in the Besu wiki (besu-eth/wiki, Performance-Stability-Memory-Allocator-Comparison.md, AWS t3.xlarge): Besu resident memory about 4.8 GiB with jemalloc vs about 9-10 GiB with glibc malloc after days to two months of running.
compiler_and_flags: jemalloc 5.3.1 'built from source', configure options, compiler and flags not stated; glibc 2.41, THP always
hardware: Vultr dedicated-vCPU VM, x86_64, 2 cores (CPU model not stated), 2026-09-13
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; default allocator in FreeBSD libc; used in Firefox per mimalloc's README
tradeoffs: Multiple arenas and size-class bins cut fragmentation and lock contention, but jemalloc is a larger tuning surface (narenas, decay_ms, percpu_arena) and the Besu test saw more minor page faults than glibc. Needs LD_PRELOAD or linking; behaviour depends on THP settings and version (jemalloc 5.3.1 here).
caveats: The jemalloc repo carries no benchmark numbers at all (README, TUNING.md and ChangeLog checked), and jemalloc.net and people.freebsd.org (home of the founding paper) were blocked in this session. The independent evidence found is a single small third-party repo (0 stars, no licence shown, raw CSVs deliberately not committed) with a modest gain on one Rails workload; the author notes MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 on glibc recovers most of the memory gap and that 5% is 'real but modest'. CPU model and jemalloc build flags are missing, so the tier is capped below A. The mimalloc-bench and mimalloc README charts include jemalloc and glibc but are SVG graphs relative to mimalloc, with jemalloc generally slower than mimalloc, so no jemalloc-vs-glibc numbers could be read from them. A founding-paper record (BSDCan 2006, jemalloc vs phkmalloc, tier B) already exists in data/wave0-seed; this record adds a modern jemalloc-vs-glibc comparison.

name: Klein
baseline: GLM (glm::quat multiplication; glm::dualquat converted with mat3x4_cast and applied to a glm::vec4), with RTM (Realtime Math) as a second reference
workload: Static llvm-mca analysis (100 iterations, dispatch width 6) of the generated SSE assembly for two routines: rotor (quaternion) composition and motor (dual-quaternion) application to a point; not measured run time.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md llvm-mca totals per 100 iterations: rotor composition Klein 821 cycles / 2400 instructions vs GLM 1522 cycles / 5700 instructions (1.85x fewer cycles, derived from page data) vs RTM 824 cycles / 2300 instructions (parity); block reciprocal throughput 8.0 vs GLM 14.0 vs RTM 7.0. Motor application to a point: Klein 1831 cycles / 5900 instructions vs GLM dual-quat 5435 cycles / 14100 instructions (2.97x fewer cycles, derived from page data); block reciprocal throughput 13.5 vs 38.5. docs/index.md: 'Klein's performance is fully competitive with state of the art kinematic and math libraries built with traditional vector and quaternion formulations.'
tradeoffs: Specialised to 3D projective geometric algebra P(R*_{3,0,1}) with SSE (SSE3 required, SSE4.1 optional) rather than a general vector library; SSE intrinsics only in this version (README requires an SSE3 processor). Points, lines, planes, rotors and motors share one algebra, so motors replace separate quaternion and dual-quaternion code.
caveats: The only numbers are first-party llvm-mca cycle estimates (the page itself warns they cannot predict real performance); no runtime measurements, compiler version, flags or target CPU are stated, and Klein's source supports mc_ruler microbenchmark builds against GLM and RTM in perf/ but no timing results are published. GLM's assembly is largely scalar with stack spills, so GLM was probably built without its SIMD options (not stated); the GLM motor-application routine includes converting a dual quaternion to a 3x4 matrix on each call, which inflates its count against Klein's direct motor-point application. Against RTM, the best-optimised SIMD baseline, the result is a tie. The project site jeremyong.com/klein, which the README points to for documentation, is blocked here; the docs were read from the repo's docs/ folder. Repo is archived, with the README saying it was paused for lack of time.
